questions.explanation: A formal region is one defined by an official act: a boundary is drawn, a name and rules are attached, and membership is a matter of being inside the line. Its boundary is sharp rather than gradual, and it can be contested precisely because it was imposed, which is why formal regions generate political argument over their edges. The distinguishing feature is the authority behind the definition, not the shape on the map. The tempting belief is that a hard boundary proves a region is real in a social sense, when a drawn line is exactly as compatible with a population that ignores it as with one that lives by it.

questions.explanation: Site is the set of physical attributes of the ground a place occupies: relief, drainage, soil, defensibility, the quality of a harbour. Situation is the relationship of that place to everything around it, so the same site can be well situated in one period and badly situated in another when routes, resources or political frontiers move. The distinction is between the intrinsic and the relational, and it explains why a site that was excellent for a medieval walled town may be poor for a modern port while the situation has changed beneath it. The tempting belief is that the two words are synonyms for location, when the whole explanatory work of the pair depends on separating them.

answer.exemplar: Proximity lowers the cost of matching buyers with sellers, of sharing infrastructure, of moving workers between jobs and of trading ideas, so a cluster lets each participant act as though a much larger market were available to it. What the cluster charges is concentrated on the residents and the users who did not gain that market access: higher rents, longer journeys, congestion and local air pollution, all of which are consequences of the cluster existing rather than costs any individual firm chose to bear. The gains are captured by the participants and the losses are spread across everybody who lives there, so the pattern persists well past the point at which it is a net gain in aggregate.

questions.explanation: Agglomeration economies are the external benefits of being near other firms: a bigger effective labour market, cheaper access to suppliers and customers, shared infrastructure, and knowledge that spills over between neighbours. None of those gains requires anyone to pay for them, so they are captured entirely by the participants. The costs work the other way round, since congestion, pollution, higher rents and longer journeys are external costs imposed on residents and users who have no stake in the cluster and no vote in its expansion. The tempting belief is that a cluster's benefits must exceed its costs because people keep choosing to be there, which confuses private returns with a social balance and is the reasoning that lets an unpriced cost accumulate for decades.
questions.hint: Ask what firms gain from proximity, then ask who pays for the congestion that follows.
questions.learningObjective: explain the benefits of agglomeration and the costs it externalises

As numbers rise the resource is overgrazed faster than it can regenerate, and once the vegetation cover is lost the collapse is not easily reversed, because the soil that holds the seed and the seedlings is itself gone. What prevents this is a rule that changes the individual calculation: a binding quota, a limit on the herd, or an enforceable right of access that can be withdrawn, each of which makes restraint privately worthwhile.

questions.explanation: The structure of the incentives is what matters. A household adding an animal captures the entire marginal gain privately, while the overgrazing it contributes is distributed across all the users of the pasture, so the private benefit is full and the private cost is a small fraction. Every household reasoning this way produces a total that is far beyond what the resource can regenerate, and the point at which it is exceeded is reached long before anyone notices. The collapse can then be self-reinforcing, since bare soil loses the seeds and the organic matter from which the cover returns. The tempting belief is that a commons collapses because people are greedy, when it collapses because the cost of restraint is private and the cost of excess is shared, which is a description of incentives rather than of character.

answer.exemplar: A climate zone is a class defined by thresholds on monthly averages of temperature and rainfall, and the underlying quantities change continuously across the surface as latitude, altitude and distance from a coast all shift. Averaging over a month smooths the weather further, so a single year at one site is a summary of many days that individually belonged to neither side of the threshold. A mapped boundary is therefore a line drawn through a gradient, and its exact position is set by the threshold chosen, the data density and the resolution of the grid, all of which are conventions. The consequence is that two places a few kilometres apart can be assigned different zones while having the same climate, and a year that is unusually wet can put a station on the other side of the line from itself.

questions.explanation: The line on a map is a convention about where to put a class boundary, and the climate does not change there. Monthly means are already averages over about thirty days of weather that each sat on one side of the threshold or the other, and moving from one zone to the next means passing through months that lie close to the boundary, which is precisely the case the threshold is least able to resolve. A second reason is that the boundary depends on where the data points are, so a densely sampled coast and a sparsely sampled interior get different apparent edges for the same climate. The tempting belief is that a mapped boundary has revealed something sharp about the world, when it has revealed something sharp about the classification that was applied.
questions.hint: Ask what a monthly mean has to average over, and what changes gradually across a distance.
questions.learningObjective: explain why boundaries between climate zones are transitional

answer.exemplar: Adaptation alters the loss from an event that will occur, and mitigation alters the event itself, so the two act on different quantities and neither can stand in for the other. A defence that avoids most of the loss this decade leaves the underlying trend running, and the trend makes the event both more frequent and eventually beyond the design capacity of the defence, so a purely adaptive strategy converges on a capital loss. Mitigation is what stops that convergence, and it is also the only measure that protects people who cannot be defended. The practical argument for doing both is therefore not a compromise between expensive options but a statement that one of them changes the terms on which the other has to keep working.

questions.explanation: The two measures act on different quantities: adaptation works on the damage, mitigation works on the cause, and there is no exchange rate between them. That matters most over time, because a defence is designed against a hazard assumed to be stationary, while the underlying trend is not, so an adaptive-only strategy eventually meets an event beyond the design condition and the capital is lost. Mitigation is the only measure that slows that trend and the only one that helps people too poor or too exposed to be defended. The tempting argument is that since adaptation protects people now and mitigation protects them later, the affordable one should be chosen, and it usually is, which is how a defended coastline ends up defending a hazard it has itself made larger.

answer.exemplar: A small-scale map draws a climate zone as a single patch, and everything inside it has been averaged into one summary, so a coastal strip with a maritime climate can sit inside a large inland zone of the same nominal class while having little in common with it. At a larger scale the averaging stops, the coastal strip separates, and the zone the data was assigned to appears to shrink, which is a change in the map's resolution rather than in the climate. The same operation explains why an urban heat island is invisible on a continental map and dominant on a city plan. The temptation is to read a patch on a small-scale map as a statement that the climate is uniform inside it, which is a statement about the scale of the data rather than about the weather.

questions.explanation: A climate class is defined on monthly averages, and those averages are calculated over an area whose size depends on the resolution of the data, so a small-scale map publishes a zone whose interior has been smoothed into one value. Enlarging the map replaces that smoothed interior with the actual variation, and the zone consequently appears to shrink and break up, which tells us about the resolution rather than about any change in climate. The same mechanism produces urban heat islands that are real in every sense and simply invisible below a certain map scale. The tempting reading is that the sharper map has discovered a difference that the coarse one missed, when in fact the coarse one never claimed the interior was uniform except by averaging it into apparent uniformity.

The protection works exactly as designed and is defeated by its own scope, which is why the management unit for a flood has to be the watershed rather than the protected area. Because vulnerability is a social condition and can change within a lifetime, the same hazard can produce a different risk in the same place. questions.explanation: Nothing can be assessed until the event is characterised, since its frequency and intensity set the scale of everything downstream, and only then is it meaningful to ask what stands in its path. Counting the exposure establishes how many people and assets are at stake at all, and the vulnerability of those units then determines how much of that count would actually be harmed, which is the step that turns a headcount into a loss. Ranking by exposure alone is the standard error, since it credits the same damage to a raised house as to a ground-floor flat. The final step, choosing between adaptation and mitigation, depends on all three terms and cannot be made before them.
questions.hint: Start with the event, then count what is in its path, then ask what state that is in.
